name: Neo-Marxism
summary: Neo-Marxism covers twentieth-century schools that keep Marx's critique of capitalism and class power but revise orthodox economics and determinism, adding culture, psychology, ideology and Weberian ideas of status and power. It explains why capitalism has persisted through consumer integration, hegemony and Keynesian management, and looks to varied agents of change rather than the industrial working class alone. Its economic strands stress monopoly capital, imperialism and dependency, and it generally rejects both liberal capitalism and Soviet-style state socialism.
scope: The post-war revival of Marxist theory that reference works and scholarship call neo-Marxism. Toscano's Blackwell Encyclopedia entry says the label was first used for the radical political economists Joan Robinson, Paul Baran and Paul Sweezy (monopoly capital, imperialism, development and underdevelopment; Foster-Carter's 1973 survey of 'neo-Marxist approaches to development and underdevelopment' belongs here), and is also applied to the Frankfurt School and similar thinkers who kept Marx's critical aims while revising orthodox Marxism for fascism and mass culture; Kellner calls the Frankfurt theorists 'neo-Marxian', and the Routledge Encyclopedia of Philosophy calls Lefebvre's humanistic Marxism neo-Marxism. Ritzer and Schubert treat analytic and post-Marxism as later developments. Includes the Frankfurt School (Horkheimer, Adorno, Marcuse) and the monopoly-capital and development strand. Excludes orthodox, Leninist and Maoist Marxism, and thinkers (Gramsci, Habermas, Althusser and others) whom Wikipedia lists but whom none of the saved defining sources names as neo-Marxist.
